Discussion 280

A carbonation-driven dynamic formation environment 281

The in situ detection of hydration in Martian carbonate phases is broadly consistent with 282

orbital infrared observations first reported in 1969 by the Mariner 6 and 7 flyby spacecraft, 283

which identified absorption features at 2.28 and 5.4 µm – diagnostic of hydrous Mg- 284

carbonate phases such as hydromagnesite (Mg₅(CO₃)₄(OH)₂·4H₂O) and artinite 285

(Mg₂(CO₃)(OH)₂·3H₂O) – primarily across the southern hemisphere (9). 286

Orbital near-infrared spectra of the Jezero region, particularly along the Margin unit near 287

Neretva Vallis, also reveal absorption bands consistent with hydrated Mg-carbonate, 288

suggesting an authigenic deposition of carbonates in a sustained aqueous environment 289

from the Noachian to early Hesperian (e.g., 8). Indeed, the orbital data are best explained 290

by hydrated Mg-carbonate (9,10), although alternative interpretations suggest the presence 291

of additional hydrated phases, such as smectite (24). By contrast, Perseverance’s in situ 292

analyses show that most Jezero carbonate phases are anhydrous and contain both Fe and 293

Mg carbonate, typically associated with olivine, hydrated Mg-sulfate and anhydrous Ca- 294

sulfate, and perchlorate, in both the crater floor and delta fan targets (21,25). This is 295

similar to the mineral assemblage observed at Amherst Point, although these targets 296

exhibit less abundant silica phases. Silica might have a stabilizing influence on hydrated 297

carbonate (26) in Amherst Point. This inconsistency suggests that orbital carbonate 298

detections (e.g., 10) may often reflect mixtures with hydrated silicate phases rather than 299

widespread hydrated carbonate, implying that pure hydrated carbonate phases are rare on 300

the Martian surface. Hydrated carbonate is not even detected in other Margin targets (13); 301

hence, it is the sole detection by any lander mission to Mars. 302

We propose that the hydrated carbonate formed through carbonation-driven precipitation, 303

with Mg/Fe carbonates replacing olivine at multiple locations in Amherst Point (Fig. 5A 304

and B). This suggests that the original olivine underwent aqueous carbonation, 305

accompanied by the formation of serpentine phases and amorphous silica (Fig. 5) (23). 306

Spatial patterns in PIXL data further document these replacement textures at sub- 307

millimeter scales, with carbonate–silicate associations (Figs. 5A and B) consistent with 308

progressive carbonation of olivine. 309

The formation of Jezero margin carbonates could include a combination of processes (10), 310

such as near-shore lacustrine carbonate precipitation and fluvial transport of detrital 311

materials, with the southern deposits most consistent with an authigenic lacustrine origin. 312

Their topographic restriction to the pre-breach shoreline elevations of Jezero Crater 313

indicates formation during an early, closed-basin phase of the paleolake, when high 314

alkalinity and shallow, Mg-rich waters favored carbonate deposition. While some 315

carbonate could have been added later or through detrital input, the mineralogy and spatial 316

trends suggest that the Marginal carbonates represent near-shore, fluvio-lacustrine 317

deposition before the outlet breach (10). 318


<!-- Page 12 -->


However, olivine carbonation provides the most plausible explanation for hydrated Mg- 319

carbonate formation, as supported by the mineralogical and geochemical evidence in Figs. 320

5A and B. It is noted that the composition of local fluid chemistry is not uniquely 321

constrained; therefore, precise replication of a localized parent fluid chemistry is not 322

possible. Our hypothesis of carbonation-driven hydrated carbonate precipitation is also 323

consistent with a new, broader Jezero Margin study of carbonated ultramafic rocks (13). 324

In a MgO–CO2–H2O system, the hydrated Mg carbonate intermediates will precipitate 325

first, because, although magnesite is thermodynamically favored, it is hindered by slow 326

kinetics (27). Mg2+ is highly soluble in water; as the Mg2+·6H2O complex (or magnesium 327

cation coordinated by six water molecules) has a high energy barrier for dehydration 328

(ΔhydG° = −1903.72 kJ mol−1) (28), the formation of hydrated Mg carbonates will precede 329

the formation of magnesite and dolomite (CaMg(CO₃)₂) (27). Direct precipitation of 330

magnesite typically requires elevated temperatures (>100°C), microbial mediation, or 331

recrystallization or dehydration of its hydrous precursors at ambient temperatures and 332

pressures (e.g., 29). An experimental heat treatment of hydrated Mg carbonates yielded a 333

transformation sequence, with increasing temperature, of: lansfordite → nesquehonite → 334

dypingite → hydromagnesite → magnesite (30). Beginning around 50°C, nesquehonite 335

begins to dehydrate with heating (31), releasing water into the system, and then the 336

structure begins to decompose around 100 °C (32). Hence, if the detected phase is similar 337

to nesquehonite (Fig. 3E), it is conceivable that it represents a persistent low-temperature 338

formation environment (19), where fluids were sufficiently alkaline (pH ~8.5–12.5) (33). 339

Amherst Point represents a chemically dynamic environment. The persistence of unaltered 340

olivine suggests temporarily limited or spatially constrained fluid flow, as extensive 341

interaction would have fully altered the olivine. The preservation of olivine alongside 342

alteration minerals suggests limited exposure or separate alteration events and points to a 343

multi-stage alteration history involving episodic or evolving fluid regimes. Elemental (Fig. 344

S1) and mineral maps from PIXL (Fig. 5) reveal similar patchy alteration patterns, 345

supporting the interpretation of localized or short-lived fluid pathways within the Eastern 346

Margin Unit. Also, PIXL phase maps (Fig. 5) show a heterogeneous distribution of 347

olivine, hydrous and anhydrous Mg/Fe carbonate and sulfate, and silica, recording a 348

complex and possibly multi-phase history of fluid-rock interaction. 349

The coexistence of hydrated and anhydrous Mg-carbonate in the same fracture system 350

(Fig. 3A and B) suggests a changing alteration environment over time. The observed co- 351

occurrence of hydrated and anhydrous Mg-carbonates suggests an initial phase of low- 352

temperature fluid activity favoring hydrated carbonate precipitation, followed by partial 353

thermal transformation to magnesite. The orbital observations of a mixture of magnesite 354

and hydrous carbonates in Jezero and its watershed could indicate the thermal 355

transformation (4). However, anhydrous carbonate is found in all olivine-containing or 356 olivine-derived lithologies in Jezero (4), and hydrated carbonate was detected only in one 357 abraded patch. Therefore, thermal transformation from hydrous to anhydrous carbonate is 358 not indicative of the general trends in the area. Carbonate minerals in Amherst Point could 359


<!-- Page 13 -->


be detrital, resulting from multiple episodes of fluid flow shown to have taken place 360 within Jezero (24). 361

Alternatively, hydrated Mg-carbonate was observed to form as weathering products on 362 meteorites found in Antarctica and has been shown to result from surficial evaporitic 363 efflorescence on the olivine grains (34). If the hydrated Mg-carbonate in Amherst Point 364 was formed via this mechanism, it would suggest that the carbonate formation period 365 could be extended further through time beyond what was previously expected. Drawing an 366 analogy from the weathering of meteorites in Antarctica (35), and although hydrated Mg- 367 carbonates are often the first carbonates to form (27), we could see a later stage of cold, 368 dry alteration where intermittent weathering episodes (potentially driven by climatic and 369 seasonal fluctuations and near-surface water inventories, 36) altered olivine into hydrated 370 Mg-carbonates, establishing a persistent weathering cycle. This mechanism represents a 371 previously underappreciated carbonate sink, gradually drawing down atmospheric CO₂ 372 beyond that accounted for by earlier models (37). In addition, separate stages of alteration 373 mineral evolution may be recorded in these rocks, with magnesite forming early in the 374 rock’s history at higher temperatures (> 100 °C), and then hydrated Mg-carbonates 375 forming later over a longer time period in the near-surface when near-freezing conditions 376 allowed for thin films of CO2-bearing water to form on the olivine grains (38), releasing 377 silica, and allowing for the formation of hydrated Mg-carbonates cannot be entirely ruled 378 out. 379

The spatial association of carbonate and sulfate suggests this diagenetic sequence was 380

followed by a late-stage infilling of hydrous and anhydrous sulfate minerals (Fig. 5A and 381

B). Late-stage fluid rock interaction could also be supported by the presence of a 382

mineralized vein crosscutting the abrasion patch (Fig. 1G), although the chemical 383

composition of this vein was not determined. Additionally, SiO₂ is primarily concentrated 384

along distinct cross-cutting vein-like structures as shown in the PIXL sol 921 phase map 385

(Fig. 5C and D), suggesting that SiO₂ emplacement is controlled by fracture permeability. 386

The localized and linear distribution of SiO2, especially where fractures intersect olivine- 387

and carbonate-rich zones, points to late-stage silica-rich fluid infiltration, likely associated 388

with a separate, chemically distinct alteration event. Of particular significance is the 389

association of hydrated Mg-carbonate with the silica veins, indicating two scenarios: 1) 390

silica was produced concomitant with mineral carbonation and hydrated carbonate 391

deposition (11), and 2) these late-stage fluids were silica-saturated and capable of 392

preserving hydrated carbonate over a prolonged period (26). The spatial zoning with 393

silica-rich cores encircled by carbonate and sulfate zones (Fig. 5B) further supports a 394

model of fluid mixing, cooling, or redox boundary-driven mineralization. Comparable 395

patterns are noted in PIXL observations, where silica-rich interiors are bordered by 396

carbonate-bearing zones (Fig. 5B), consistent with mineralization influenced by 397

geochemical gradients (23). 398

Likewise, the detection of perchlorate within the shallow subsurface of the Amherst Point 399

target (instead of the surficial oxidative environment) suggests a late-stage oxidative fluid 400


<!-- Page 14 -->


infiltration similar to the observations of Jezero crater floor (39) and even in Gale crater 401

(40). Perchlorate is concomitantly present with both hydrous and anhydrous sulfate in the 402

vein area (Figs. 3 and 5), suggesting that sulfates formed alongside perchlorate or 403

precursor chlorine-bearing salts in briny fluids later oxidized to perchlorate, marking a 404

separate step in the geochemical timeline. 405

Prolonged shallow subsurface preservation of hydrated carbonate 406

That metastable hydrated Mg-carbonate remains detectable in Martian shallow 407

subsurface settings is intriguing. The abrasion at Amherst Point reaches a depth of 408

approximately 1 cm (deeper than other abrasions), where the hydrated Mg-carbonate was 409

previously preserved in the subsurface. Thermal modeling and experimental constraints 410 indicate that Mars’s diurnal thermal skin depth, which defines how deeply the daily 411 temperature cycle penetrates the surface, is ~4-5 cm for typical regolith parameters (e.g., 412

grain size, porosity, and thermal inertia) (41-43). Thus, preservation of hydrated Mg- 413 carbonate even at 1 cm below the surface suggests that 1) daily temperature fluctuation 414 (44) is already significantly reduced or is almost negligible at this depth, 2) the Martian 415 regolith is an efficient thermal insulator even over 1.5 cm depth (43) to prevent mineral 416 dehydration, and 3) Martian shallow subsurface (1.5 cm) is frigid (mean temperature 417 ~-30 °C) (43), which can drastically reduce the rate of dehydration (see Supplementary 418 Text) (45 and references therein). 419

The kinetic factors of hydrated Mg-carbonate transformation under Mars surface or 420

shallow subsurface conditions are not well known, and therefore, modelling of the 421

formation and preservation is difficult at this time. Metastable hydrated carbonates like 422

lansfordite and nesquehonite are prone to dehydrating into dypingite or hydromagnesite 423

over timescales of days at ~50–60 °C (31). According to the Arrhenius equation (see 424

Supplementary Text), the low thermal energy exponentially suppresses reaction kinetics. 425

The activation energy for this transformation in the presence of silica is reported to 426

be ~64.9 kJ mol⁻¹ (26), and although it varies across studies (e.g., 46), we adopt this value 427

because abundant silica is also present in Amherst Point (see Fig. 5C and D). 428

Extrapolating this behavior to Martian shallow subsurface conditions (~–30 °C) (43) and 429

applying the Arrhenius relationship implies that such transformations would be 430

suppressed by several thousand times relative to laboratory conditions, extending 431

timescales from days to effectively geological time scales. If the detected hydrated 432

carbonate is similar to nesquehonite (Fig. 3E), it suggests that it did not fully transform 433

into dypingite or hydromagnesite (19) in those locations. Hence, the Martian shallow- 434

subsurface environment dramatically slows or effectively “freezes” the transformation 435

process. 436

Additionally, surface radiation appears to be mitigated entirely at shallow depths, 437 allowing for long-term stability of hydration. In a Mars simulation chamber experiment 438


<!-- Page 15 -->


(47), hydrated Mg-carbonate, such as hydromagnesite, was exposed to low pressures 439

(from 660 Pa to ~1 Pa), a CO₂-dominated atmosphere, UV radiation, and a temperature of 440

~25°C for more than 25 days. They observed no significant changes in water-related 441

absorption bands (in the near-infrared spectrum), indicating that the hydromagnesite had 442

not dehydrated. Although exposure to Martian surface conditions in the laboratory does 443

not fully replicate the billions of years of environmental exposure on Mars, SHERLOC 444

typically analyzes the freshly exposed surface of abraded rock approximately 36 hours 445

after the rover makes the abrasion (48). This brief exposure time suggests that the 446

hydrated Mg-carbonate at Amherst Point was likely not subjected to prolonged contact 447

(e.g., fewer than 25 days) with the Martian atmosphere, allowing it to remain stable and 448

detectable by the SHERLOC instrument. It is possible that even shallow subsurface 449

shielding likely contributed to maintaining the mineral's stability prior to abrasion (48). 450

Subsurface shielding of hydrated phases appears to be the most plausible explanation; 451

however, the current Mars atmosphere does not remove all water from minerals even on 452

the surface. SuperCam on board Perseverance sees hydration bands on natural surface 453

targets (48,49), but we do not know their initial hydration state (including 454

adsorbed/absorbed H2O) or how quickly they transform into other mineral phases. 455

SuperCam also often observes deeper H2O absorption bands in the infrared (1.9 µm) in 456

abrasions vs natural surface targets (25,49). However, SuperCam measures bulk 457

hydration in the infrared because the rocks are composed of multiple minerals (such as 458

phyllosilicates, sulfates, and carbonates) and the hydration cannot be confidently assigned 459

to a single phase. Therefore, SHERLOC’s high spatial resolution analyses, with a 100 µm 460

spot size (15), help identify phases that might otherwise be missed. In any case, water in 461

hydrated Mg-carbonate minerals is structurally bound within the crystal lattice, which 462

would have made it resistant to loss under Mars' surface or shallow subsurface conditions 463

(50). 464

The preservation of hydrated carbonate likely reflects a combination of textural and 465

geochemical stabilization processes. PIXL phase maps (Fig. 5, A and B) reveal hydrated 466

Mg-carbonate spatially associated with silica veins. Dissolved silica in aqueous media is 467

known to influence the interfacial stability of nesquehonite, lowering its nucleation 468

barrier and enhancing resistance to transformation into hydromagnesite (26). In addition 469

to silica, the fine-scale variability of coexisting hydrous and anhydrous magnesium 470

sulfates within a few hundred microns suggests that these phases may have contributed to 471

maintaining hydration in carbonates. Sulfate ions in natural brines can reduce the rate of 472

magnesite precipitation by promoting dissolution of hydrated Mg-carbonate and forming 473

strong MgSO₄ aqueous complexes, thereby limiting the availability of free Mg²⁺ (51). 474

Laboratory studies further indicate that coexisting phases can modulate the hydration– 475

dehydration kinetics of precipitated sulfates, favoring hydrated sulfate phases that are not 476

in thermodynamic equilibrium (52). Moreover, the transformation from nesquehonite to 477


<!-- Page 16 -->


hydromagnesite can be suppressed under Ca²⁺-poor, Mg²⁺-rich conditions (31, 51), even 478

under inert atmospheric conditions (pH₂O = pCO₂ = 10⁻⁴ mbar) at subzero temperatures 479

(53). This aligns with the PIXL-derived chemistry from Amherst Point and the inferred 480

restoration of a nesquehonite-like phase (Fig. 5 and Fig. S1). Micro-scale interactions 481

with hygroscopic perchlorate and phosphate-rich fluid may have also helped preserve 482

hydration in carbonates via micro-localized humidity modulation and protective surface 483

coatings (54-56). However, direct evidence for the role of these physicochemical 484

parameters in long-term preservation of hydration in carbonates on Mars is lacking and 485

warrants future experimental testing. 486

Overall, a spatially limited and localized presence of hydrated Mg-carbonates is expected 487

for such metastable minerals. Their long-term preservation, therefore, indicates 488

exceptional local boundary conditions of Amherst Point – specifically, water-rich, 489

alkaline chemistry combined with effective thermal and diagenetic shielding in the 490

shallow subsurface. A localized long-term preservation of metastable phases, thus, could 491

be a defining feature for Martian mineral discoveries that reflect environmental 492

heterogeneity rather than rarity of formation. As such, this occurrence provides a 493

uniquely sensitive record of ancient aqueous geochemistry and shallow subsurface 494

preservation aspects, strengthening its significance for understanding Mars’s CO₂ cycling 495

and unappreciated hydrated niches. 496

Hydrous phases and redox diversity as windows into early Jezero habitability 497

The presence of hydrated carbonate and sulfate implies that the local Jezero environment 498

was once CO₂-rich and contained liquid water, supporting the notion that the crater 499

hosted a warm and wet environment during the late Noachian (~4 to 3.7 Gya), a time 500

when early life was emerging on Earth (e.g., 57). Hydrated magnesium carbonates are 501

particularly diagnostic of alkaline conditions and indicate sustained water–rock 502

interaction in the presence of Mg and dissolved CO₂ (10). Laboratory studies show that 503

these hydrated phases preferentially form and persist under low-ionic-strength waters, 504

whereas magnesites are favored at higher salinities (51), highlighting a geochemical 505

context of their detection. Importantly, low ionic strength is also regarded as more 506

conducive to habitability (58). Taken together, newly discovered hydrated carbonate on 507

Mars suggests that this site may have preserved unusually low-salinity aqueous 508

environments, capable of sustaining liquid water even into the late Hesperian, when most 509

other regions of Mars had already dried (~3.6 Gya), although it became patchy and 510

discontinuous (59). 511

The coexistence of olivine and hydrous and anhydrous carbonates (Figs. 3A and B) 512

points to carbonation and serpentinization reactions, which not only buffer fluid 513

chemistry but also generate hydrogen and enhance redox gradients, widening the 514


<!-- Page 17 -->


potential window for habitable conditions on early Mars (60). This mineral assemblage 515

also indicates incomplete or episodic alteration, consistent with a multi-stage fluid 516

history. Hydrous carbonates are especially significant in this context, as their low- 517

temperature formation pathways are less destructive and more conducive to preserving 518

textural or chemical biosignatures (22). Silica and carbonates precipitated during 519

carbonation (22), as can be inferred from hydrated carbonates localized within silica 520

veins in Amherst Point (Fig. 5B), can preserve organics in low-temperature, water-rock 521

reaction conditions (61). However, co-occurrence of anhydrous carbonates likely reflects 522

later thermal maturation or dehydration, marking a shift from earlier clement conditions 523

to drier, less favorable environments. Together, these carbonate–silica vein and hydrous 524

and anhydrous mineral assemblages provide a mineralogical archive of evolving surface 525

and shallow-subsurface aqueous conditions. 526

The spatial association of sulfate, phosphate, and perchlorate alongside olivine, silica, 527

and both hydrous and anhydrous Mg-carbonates within the bedrock points to a 528

geochemical system containing both oxidants and reductants, nutrient sources, and 529

reservoirs of carbon – ingredients broadly consistent with the potential for diverse redox 530

and metabolic pathways. Sulfates represent a potential electron acceptor in microbial 531

redox metabolism, supporting processes such as sulfate reduction that are central to 532

anaerobic life, while phosphates are indispensable as structural components of nucleic 533

acids and energy carriers in biological systems (e.g., 62,63). Perchlorates, although 534

strongly oxidizing and capable of imposing oxidative stress on organics (64), can 535

paradoxically aid in their preservation under cold and dry conditions, and are also known 536

to serve as terminal electron acceptors for specialized microorganisms on Earth (e.g., 537

65,66). 538

However, the mere presence of such phases does not demonstrate that any such redox 539

reactions actually occurred; rather, it indicates that the chemical precursors necessary for 540

habitability (five out of six essential elements of life-as-we-know-it: Carbon, Hydrogen, 541

Nitrogen, Oxygen, Phosphorus, and Sulfur or CHNOPS) were present in this 542

microenvironment. In other words, the mineralogical associations captured at Amherst 543

Point represent a preserved record of the conditions that could have sustained 544

habitability, even if redox activity never took place. 545

Overall, water–rock reaction–driven carbonation would have been active locally under a 546

CO₂-rich atmosphere (5) when the ancient Jezero crater margin hosted warm, alkaline 547

waters long enough to form hydrated Mg-carbonate. The local Jezero environment could 548

have supported habitability during this interval in the late Noachian to early Hesperian 549

(~3.8–3.6 Ga). Thereafter, conditions likely shifted as Mars progressively lost CO₂ and 550

water potentially through carbonate formation post–3.5 Ga (6). Although this discovery 551

of hydrated Mg-carbonate alone cannot reconcile the missing-carbonate problem (6), it 552


<!-- Page 18 -->


provides a critical link between orbital detections and surface processes. Most 553

importantly, since then, the local shallow subsurface conditions within the Margin unit 554

may have remained stable, preserving the minerals’ hydration state. The preservation of 555

carbonate hydrate further indicates that the Amherst Point rock did not experience 556

elevated temperatures (due to metamorphism, hydrothermalism, or deep burial, etc.). 557

Rather, the hydrated carbonates represent relics of ancient fluid–rock interactions in a 558

shallow-subsurface environment. In any case, the discovery expands the surface 559

inventory of carbonate phases on Mars and offers new evidence of Mars’s long-missing 560

CO2 sink (6). 561

Mars sample return 562

The Amherst Point abrasion target – an aqueously-deposited clastic rock containing 563

silica, phosphate, sulfate, and most importantly, carbonate minerals preserved in their 564

hydration states – provided the incentive to acquire the first rock core sample of the 565

Margin unit named “Pelican Point” (Fig. 1F) (Sample 22, drilled on sol 923) (67) for 566

potential future return to Earth. The oriented core contains materials that can address 567

pressing questions about the early Mars atmosphere and habitability. Sample return will 568

allow isotopic analyses of water and volatiles in aqueously altered minerals present in the 569

workspace to help reconstruct the hydrological cycles and atmospheric processes during 570

the deposition of the eastern Margin unit, offering new insights into Jezero’s evolving 571

habitability (12 and references therein). Especially, if the nesquehonite-like phase did not 572

entirely dehydrate into hydromagnesite (Fig. 3E and Table S1) and thereby did not 573

release captured CO2 (31), its isotopic composition could turn out to be a time capsule for 574

early Mars’ climate. Isotopic geochronology of the spatially associated mineral phases 575

present will constrain the timing of their alteration and deposition. Additionally, the 576

determination of the crystal structure, including the hydration states of the detected 577

metastable hydrated Mg-carbonate, would reflect the stability under certain pH, Eh, 578

salinity, and temperature conditions. Jezero’s aqueous environment was episodic, and 579

therefore, only low concentrations of organics are expected (12). While carbonates may 580

preserve biosignatures (68), their abundance could remain below the detection limits of in 581

situ instruments onboard the Perseverance rover (1). Consequently, detailed chemical, 582

morphological, and isotopic analyses of the returned Margin sample will be imperative 583

for advancing astrobiological understanding of Jezero crater’s ancient lake margin. 584

Materials and Methods 585

Laboratory synthesis and characterization of nesquehonite 586

The nesquehonite sample was synthesized following the solution stoichiometry described 587

in (69) for sample 2, which yielded high crystallinity and pure nesquehonite phase, unlike 588

sample 1. The resulting solution was allowed to stand in clean Petri dishes (3 inches wide) 589

and evaporate on the lab bench. On the fourth day of the solution evaporation, relatively 590


<!-- Page 19 -->


elongated needle-like crystals were observed in the center of the Petri dishes and picked 591

up for Raman spectroscopy and XRD analyses to confirm the purity of the mineral (Fig. 592

S5). Raman spectra and images were acquired using the WITec α-Scanning Near-Field 593

Optical Microscope (alpha 300) optimized to incorporate confocal Raman spectroscopic 594

imaging utilizing a ×50 Long Working Distance (LWD) and a ×5 LWD objective lenses. 595

The signal was acquired by accumulating each Raman spectrum and repeated 40 times for 596

10 s exposure time at a 488 nm laser excitation wavelength using a 600 g/mm grating. The 597

resulting spectrum was exported to TrueMatch Raman Spectral Database 598

(https://raman.oxinst.com/products/software/truematch) to match and verify the 599

nesquehonite peak positions. Also, the crystalline material was powdered and used for 600

XRD for phase characterization. The XRD analysis was conducted on a Bruker D8 601

diffractometer equipped with a Cu source (λ = 1.5406 Å), a 2mm collimator, and a 602

VÅNTEC-500 area detector. Image plates were processed into 1D patterns using the 603

DIFFRAC.EVA software. XRD data were refined using structures obtained from the 604

International Center for Diffraction Data (ICDD) structural database PDF-4+. 605

SHERLOC spectroscopy and imaging 606

SHERLOC utilizes a combination of deep ultraviolet (DUV) Raman and native 607

fluorescence spectroscopy for a high-sensitivity detection of various organic molecules 608

and minerals (15). The instrument focuses a 248.6 nm DUV pulsed laser beam of a 100 609

μm spot size on a targeted surface to generate map scans, which can be co-registered onto 610

images from the autofocus context imager (ACI). The ACI obtains greyscale images of the 611

desired target, with a pixel resolution of 10.1 μm/pixel, from a ~4.8 cm standoff distance. 612

The instrument can identify where the laser is focused within the greyscale ACI images, 613

allowing the correlation of spectroscopic and textural features on the target to understand 614

their fine-scale spatial distributions and provenance. A second imaging system, the Wide 615

Angle Topographic Sensor for Operations and eNgineering (WATSON), acquires color 616

images of the desired target at resolutions down to 13 μm/pixel from standoff distances 617

ranging between 2.5 and 40 cm and provides a broader context for the target rocks and 618

geological formations (15). The WATSON and ACI images can be co-registered and 619

combined to create a composite image called a “colorized ACI” (70). 620

Abrasion operations and SHERLOC scans 621

Upon identification of a target of scientific interest using Perseverance's remote science 622

instruments (e.g., MastCam-Z, SuperCam) (1), the surfaces are abraded using an abrasion 623

tool designed to remove the surface layer of the rocks. The resulting dust residues are then 624

blown away by the gaseous Dust Removal Tool (gDRT) to expose flat and smooth rock 625

surfaces (a circular patch 15 mm deep and 45 mm wide) for subsequent SHERLOC and 626

PIXL proximity science observations. Abrasion operations are followed by SHERLOC 627

spectroscopy scans for scientific analysis that include 1) HDR scans rastering the laser 628

over a 7×7 mm area, 2) survey scan rastering the laser over a 5×5 mm area, and 3) detail 629

scan rastering the laser over a 1×1 mm area. 630

Spectral data processing 631

Preliminary data processing for a SHERLOC observation of the Amherst Point abrasion 632

target (sol 921) in the Margin unit was carried out using an open-source software tool 633

called Loupe, developed at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (71). The software provides 634

several essential features, such as dark frame subtraction, laser normalization, and 635

selecting ROIs and correlating them with locations on the ACI image. To better evaluate 636

the SHERLOC observations, spectral data were exported from the Loupe package and 637

converted to be compatible with WITec’s Suite SIX software environment 638

(https://raman.oxinst.com/products/software/witec-software-suite) using a Python script 639

written by K. Uckert. The script used the Loupe dataset to generate an ASCII file that is 640

converted into .wip format using the WITec—ASCIItoWIPConverterApp package. 641

Raman Error Calculations 642

Raman peak position errors were calculated following the methods described by (18). The 643

error associated with band fitting was estimated using the methods of Lenz and Ayres 644

(72). The band fitting error was then combined with the error in instrument calibration 645

curves (±1.8 cm-1 for SHERLOC) (73) using a root square sum to estimate the total error 646

in peak position. The bands were fitted to a Gaussian function using Grams/AI software 647

(Thermo Fisher Scientific). 648

SHERLOC analogue instrument operations 649

The reference spectra from lab-synthesized nesquehonite presented here were collected on 650

a SHERLOC analogue instrument housed at Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which is a deep 651

UV Raman and fluorescence spectrometer that uses a similar optical path, components, 652

and identical excitation to SHERLOC (15). Samples were placed on a clean aluminum 653

wafer and analyzed in air in ambient laboratory conditions. A 3×3 map of 100 μm annular 654

points was collected on the sample with an average laser energy of ~4.14 μJ/pulse. 655

Fluorescence data were collected with 25 pulses per point, 20 Amps; Raman data were 656

collected with 300 pulses per point. Data were laser normalized and cosmic rays were 657

removed using Loupe (https://github.com/nasa/Loupe), then calibration correction was 658

applied using a custom Python script with data collected from an Hg lamp and an 659

acetonitrile standard. The DUV Raman spectra of artinite, dypingite, and hydromagnesite 660

were collected on the SHERLOC analogue instrument Analogue Complementary Raman 661

for Operations oN Mars (ACRONM). The ACRONM instrument is modeled after the 662

MOBIUS SHERLOC prototype instrument (74) and contains a similar 248.6 nm laser and 663

the same detector as SHERLOC. ACRONM spectra were collected using a 20Hz laser 664

pulse rep rate with each spectrum being the average of six, 10-second spectra for a total 665

accumulation time of 60 seconds, and total pulse count per spectrum of 1200. Numerous 666

Raman spectra of each sample were collected at different sample locations to gauge 667

sample heterogeneity, and spectra were averaged to improve the signal-to-noise ratio. 668

ACRONM data were processed using Grams/AI software. Data processing included 669

wavenumber calibration against a cyclohexane standard, cosmic ray removal, and spectral 670


<!-- Page 21 -->


averaging. The DUV Raman spectra of magnesium carbonate hydrate (with unknown 671

hydration state) were collected by the Photon Systems RPL200 instrument located at 672

INAF-Astrophysical Observatory of Arcetri, a description of which can be found in (75). 673

PIXL operations and data processing 674

PIXL performs X-ray fluorescence (XRF) and multispectral analyses of rocks and 675

regoliths using its optical fiducial system (OFS) (16,76). The OFS captures images of the 676

target using a micro-context camera (MCC) while flashing LEDs of near-IR (723 ± 10 677

nm), green (523 ± 13 nm), blue (447 ± 4 nm), and ultraviolet (385 ± 4 nm) wavelengths, 678

respectively. The images were radiometrically corrected using color calibration targets 679

(77). The XRF analysis is conducted by rastering an X-ray beam with a diameter of 0.12 680

mm at 8 keV energy, produced by an X-ray source operated at 28 kV, over the target at a 681

0.125 mm step. X-rays produced via the interaction of the primary beam and the target are 682

measured by two Silicon Drift detectors (SDDs), each on either side of the X-ray source. 683

Collected spectra are processed to estimate elemental abundances as oxides (ex., Al as 684

Al2O3, Fe as FeO, etc.) at each analytical spot in the scanned target using PIQUANT, a 685

calibrated fundamental parameters model (78). The PIXLISE visualization tool is used to 686

perform co-registration and collaborative analyses of optical and X-ray data (16). In 687

addition, post-quantification routines are applied in PIXLISE to correct elemental 688

abundances for spectral effects related to rock surface orientation and diffraction from 689

crystalline materials (79). On the Amherst Point abrasion patch, PIXL collected MCC 690

multispectral data and conducted two 5mm × 7mm scans on 920 and 921, respectively. 691

For both scans, the step size is 0.125 mm, amounting to 2337 points in each scan. At each 692

point, the X-ray signals were collected for 10 s by each SSD detector. 693

Mineral phase abundances were estimated from quantified and corrected elemental 694

abundances by mineral stripping analysis (79,80). Briefly, candidate minerals were 695

identified based on stoichiometric similarity to endmembers in compositional mixing 696

arrays, starting with binary minerals having distinctive compositions (e.g., phosphate and 697

sulfate minerals) and progressing to more complex minerals or minerals potentially 698

forming mixtures difficult to distinguish by elemental composition (e.g., Mg, Fe-bearing 699

silicates, and carbonates). The maximum possible mineral abundance was calculated at 700

each analytical spot with each candidate identification and expressed as a percentage of all 701

quantified oxides. Resultant abundance distributions were compared with context images 702

and maps of combinations of diffraction peaks to verify that estimated minerals correlated 703

with color variations, coherent regions with distinctive diffraction patterns, or other 704

indications of grain boundaries. Quantified oxides contributing to the identified mineral 705

were then subtracted from the total inventory at each analytical spot, and the process was 706

repeated for the next mineral. For the Amherst Point target, identified minerals were, in 707

order: chlorapatite [Ca5(PO4)3Cl], calcium sulfate (CaSO4), magnesium/iron sulfate 708

[(Mg,Fe)SO4], halite (NaCl), feldspar [Cax(Na,K)1-xAl1+xSi3-xO8], augite [Cax(Mg,Fe)1- 709


<!-- Page 22 -->


xSi2O6; 0.2 ≤ x ≤ 0.5], olivine [(Mg,Fe)2SiO4], fine carbonate [(Ca,Mg,Fe)CO3], 710

serpentine-hisingerite minerals [(Mg,Fe)3xFe2(1-y)Al2ySi2O5∙nH2O; 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1 – x, 711

0 ≤ n ≤ 2], and coarse carbonate [(Ca,Mg,Fe)CO3]. Note that calculations did not 712

explicitly include elements with atomic numbers less than Na. The maximum potential 713

amount of fine carbonate was proxied by the intensity of backscattered X-rays detected 714

around the Rh Lγ by both PIXL detectors (117). The maximum potential amount of coarse 715

carbonate was proxied by 100 – TOTAL, where TOTAL is the analytical total (the sum of 716

estimated oxide abundances). In both cases, the actual carbonate mineral abundance 717

estimated was constrained by the availability of remaining CaO, MgO, and FeO. Total 718

carbonate mineral abundances were the sum of fine and coarse carbonate minerals. 719

Carbonate mineral identifications were tested by testing negative correlations between 720

analytical totals and inferred carbonate mineral abundances. Where overlapping data were 721

available, PIXL identifications were also cross-checked with SHERLOC identifications. 722

Finally, the abundances of feldspar, pyroxene, and olivine were summed for mapping the 723

distribution of primary silicates. 724

Using a Raman spectrometer onboard the Perseverance rover, we report the heterogeneous distribution of organic carbon within mudstones located in an ancient river valley on Mars. Measurements of two mudstones show hundreds of organic detections, making this the most robust organic detection in Jezero crater thus far, and, to our knowledge, the only detection of macromolecular carbon on a natural rock surface on Mars. Spectra of the interior of one rock reveal an association of organics with secondary carbonate and sulfate minerals, whereas another rock exhibits an association of organics with primary silicate-­dominated matrix. Although in situ Raman analyses cannot determine whether these organics denote abiotic or biotic sources, the organic association with both depositional and diagenetic minerals and the detection of organics on the martian surface suggests that the organics observed ubiquitously at the Bright Angel outcrop may be resistant to radiation and oxidation or have been relatively recently exposed.

INTRODUCTION The Mars Perseverance rover has been exploring Jezero crater since 2021, characterizing the geology of the region, searching for signs of ancient life, and collecting samples for possible future return to Earth (1). The detection and characterization of organic carbon on Mars is a critical component of assessing whether Mars ever harbored life. The 1976 Viking lander gas chromatograph–mass spectrometry experiments marked the first in situ search for organic compounds on Mars (2). Since Viking, the Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) Curiosity rover’s Sample Analysis at Mars instrument has detected organic carbon in bulk measurements of sedimentary rocks at Gale crater (3–6), and multi­ple reservoirs of organic matter have been inferred (5). In addition, laboratory analyses using Raman mapping techniques have revealed the

spatial associations between minerals and organic carbon in martian meteorites (7, 8), carbonaceous chondrites (9), and ureilite meteorites (10). Here, we report robust in situ, noncontact, spatially resolved organic carbon detections on Mars by Raman spectroscopic mapping. The organic carbon detected is located within fine-­grained sedimentary rocks and exhibits mineralogical and textural associations. In addition, we observe distinct organic carbon spectral features on natural rock surfaces and abraded surfaces that expose the interior of the rock. We analyze the Raman G-­band spatial distributions across the four targets analyzed at the “Bright Angel” outcrop, and compare the calculated Raman G-­band peak characteristics to those of meteorites, terrestrial samples, and synthetic standards to constrain the nature of the organic carbon.

The Scanning Habitable Environments with Raman and Luminescence for Organics and Chemicals (SHERLOC) instrument is a deep-­ultraviolet (DUV; 248.6 nm) Raman and fluorescence mapping spectrometer and context imager on the end of the Perseverance rover’s robotic arm (11). Monochromatic and full-­color images are obtained using SHERLOC’s two cameras, the Autofocus and Context Imager (ACI) and the Wide Angle Topographic Sensor for Operations and eNgineering (WATSON), respectively. WATSON images can be used to colorize ACI images to generate a high-­ resolution (10.1 μm/pixel) image that captures both color and texture for spectral context (11). SHERLOC generates spectral maps of organics and minerals colocated with context images to determine their spatial relationships with a spectral resolution as fine as 110 μm per pixel using DUV Raman scattering and/or fluorescence within the range of 800 to 4000 cm−1 and 265 to 355 nm, respectively (11). The Raman region between ~1350 and 1650 cm−1 covers a variety of vibrational modes associated with functional groups of organic compounds (12), including D-­ and G-­bands of macromolecular carbon (MMC), which occur at ~1350 and ~1600 cm−1, respectively [e.g., (13, 14)]. MMC is a solid, cross-­linked network of primarily reduced carbon that is resistant to chemical and thermal decomposition and is insoluble and nonlabile (12, 15, 16). MMC may have different degrees of structural order (17) and includes aromatic and aliphatic structures that may have substituted heteroatoms or functional groups. We note that, in general, the use of the term “MMC” serves to avoid implications of biogenicity, whereas the terms “kerogen” and “bitumen” typically implicate past life or a biogenic source (15). The G-­band (graphitic band) is attributed to the E2g symmetry in-­plane bond-­stretching motion of sp2 bonded C atom pairs, and the D-­band (defect/disorder band) derives from the A1g symmetry ring breathing mode of six-­member carbon rings (17). The G-­band peak position and bandwidth have been correlated to a variety of structural parameters of MMC including bond order and lattice strain (17, 18). Prior SHERLOC observations of fluorescence within rock targets on the Jezero crater floor may be attributable to organics; however, several inorganic sources with similar fluorescence signals complicate such assignments (19–21). Notably, a Raman G-­band was previously detected on the crater floor; however, this detection was limited to a single point within a SHERLOC map (20). Here, we report the detection of organics in multiple ancient riverbed rock targets with dozens of detections observed in each target. We also demonstrate positive and negative control results for calibration targets interrogated during this campaign.

Neretva Vallis, Jezero crater On mission sol 1159 (martian days elapsed since rover landing), Perseverance began exploring Neretva Vallis, an ancient river channel that served as the primary inlet to Jezero crater’s western margin (Fig. 1A). The Bright Angel outcrop, located on the northern side of the channel, features light-­toned, well-­layered rocks in contact with the topographically higher deposits of the Jezero crater Margin unit (Fig. 1, A and B). The exposed outcrop was likely deposited within the channel by fluvial or lacustrine processes, but the outcrop’s relative geologic age compared to other units in Jezero crater is not currently well constrained (22, 23). From sols 1180 to 1218, the SHERLOC instrument collected 18 spectral maps (totaling 1800 spectra) from four targets across three rocks of Bright Angel (Table 1). Targets included (i) the “Cheyava Falls” dust-­cleared natural surface, (ii) the “Apollo Temple” abrasion, (iii) the “Steamboat Mountain” abrasion, and (iv) the

“Walhalla Glades” abrasion (Fig. 1 and Table 1). The Cheyava Falls and Apollo Temple targets are ~16 cm apart on the Cheyava Falls rock within the “Beaver Falls” workspace, located near the contact with the Margin unit (Fig. 1, C and D) (23). The Steamboat Mountain target is on a darker-­toned rock adjacent to the Cheyava Falls rock at the Beaver Falls workspace and closer to the Margin unit contact (Fig. 1, C to E) (23). The Walhalla Glades target is ~111 m south of the Beaver Falls workspace (Fig. 1, B and F).

RESULTS Texture and color We define “texture” as the characteristics of rock grains, including their size, shape, and spatial arrangement. We also use color and tonal descriptors to better differentiate these fine-­grained rocks. The Cheyava Falls natural surface target is a fine-­grained mudstone (≤30-­μm grains), the average grain size of which is at or below the resolution of SHERLOC’s ACI (10.1 μm/pixel) (11). The reddish matrix contains discrete irregularly shaped spots (~0.25 to 1.2 mm), which have discontinuous black rims and pale interiors (Fig. 1G). These features are flush with the rock surface and contrast sharply with cross-­cutting, erosionally resistant whitish veins, which are observed throughout the Cheyava Falls rock (Fig. 1, D and G). The Apollo Temple abrasion (7.8-­mm abrasion depth) reveals the matrix to be fine grained with dark brown and black, silt-­ to fine sand-­sized grains (~30 to 400 μm) (Fig. 1, D and H, and fig. S1A). Veins are visible in the abrasion patch, and a large pit in the abrasion patch corresponds to a vein observed on the natural surface (fig. S1A). The Steamboat Mountain abrasion target (6.8-­mm abrasion depth) is darker toned and reveals a coarser-­grained texture consisting of medium sand to gravel-­sized grains (~425 μm to 2.5 mm) with greenish centers and light-­toned rims surrounded by a fine-­grained reddish matrix (Fig. 1, C, E, and I, and fig. S2). The Walhalla Glades abrasion target (7.0-­mm abrasion depth) exhibits a very fine-­grained light-­ toned matrix with black silt-­ to fine sand-­sized (~30 to 220 μm) grains distributed relatively homogeneously throughout the matrix (Fig. 1, F and J, and fig. S1B). Details regarding WATSON and ACI imaging observations for each target are provided in tables S1 and S2.

Minerals Each SHERLOC spectroscopy measurement at the Bright Angel out­ crop covers a 1 mm by 1 mm area, which allows for the characterization of the spatial distribution of minerals and organics (Table 1). Carbonate and sulfate detections with peak centers at ~1080 cm−1 and ~1013 to 1033 cm−1, respectively, are dispersed throughout the Apollo Temple matrix (Fig. 2, A and B, and fig. S3). A subset of Apollo Temple spectra contains a stronger ~1080-­cm−1 carbonate peak, revealing mineral heterogeneity within the target (Fig. 2A and fig. S4). Few carbonate and sulfate detections were made in the Walhalla Glades and Cheyava Falls matrices compared to Apollo Temple. Detections of a potential phosphate peak (a narrow band centered at ~970 cm−1) occur in the Apollo Temple and Walhalla Glades targets and may be associated with the dark-­toned grains at Walhalla Glades (fig. S5 and S4). Detections of phosphate are corroborated by colocated x-­ray fluorescence (XRF) scans of the same areas collected by the Planetary Instrument for X-­ray Lithochemistry (PIXL) (24). A broad asymmetrical Raman feature between ~950 and 1250 cm−1 with a peak center at ~1050 cm−1 is present in all mean spectra of SHERLOC maps of targets on the Bright Angel outcrop except

The ~1050-­cm−1 feature is consistent with silicate mineral phases such as igneous glass and/or feldspar (25). We note that the Raman signal for olivine, at ~835 to 845 cm−1 (28, 29), coincides with a broad background peak centered at ~800 cm−1 that is attributed to the SHERLOC optics (30).

Macromolecular carbon A heterogeneously distributed Raman band with a peak center at ~1600 cm−1 was detected within the fine-­grained matrix of rocks at Bright Angel. The band is present in the mapped mean and median. We report the peak characteristics derived from the trimmed mean (mean

spectrum after removing highest and lowest 5% of values) of select spectral maps, and in some cases, in subsets of maps associated with specific Raman features (Table 2 and Fig. 2). The highest-­intensity ~1600-­cm−1 peak was observed in the sol 1217 Apollo Temple abrasion (Fig. 3B), where the spectra were acquired when the instrument was closest to the ideal focus position for Bright Angel outcrop measurements (SHERLOC focus is described in the “Spectroscopy data acquisition” section and reported in Table 1). As detailed in Materials and Methods, we considered a wide range of other potential sources of, and contributions to, the ~1600 cm−1 feature observed in the rocks of Bright Angel. We explored the possibility of instrument background, inorganic Raman peak contributions from minerals and hydration, and terrestrial organic contamination. Ultimately, we found that these alternative hypotheses cannot fully account for the observed 1600-­cm−1 feature, giving us confidence in the G-­band assignment. We conclude that MMC is the most parsimonious explanation for this feature.

DISCUSSION The noncontact, in situ spatially resolved detection of MMC on Mars with Raman spectroscopy provides an unambiguous confirmation and corroboration of previous reports of organics on Mars. Previous work used temperature-­controlled pyrolysis and combustion experiments on the Curiosity rover to reveal organics, including macromolecules, in drilled samples from Gale crater (3–6). DUV Raman

spectroscopy is highly complementary to the mass spectrometry measurements of Curiosity, yielding an independent detection of organics in a different region of Mars. SHERLOC measurements at Bright Angel mark a robust detection of spatially resolved MMC with Raman spectroscopy and, to our knowledge, the only detection of organics on a dust-­cleared, but otherwise unprepared martian surface. SHERLOC’s detection of organics in a mudstone outside of Gale crater suggests that organics may have been more than just locally present and may have been more widely available in ancient (~3.5 Gyr) lakes and rivers on Mars. Raman spectra alone cannot determine biogenicity, but emplacement and formation processes may be inferred from G-­band parameters and mineral or textural associations. Below, we consider the nature, including possible sources and alteration histories, of the MMC at Bright Angel.

Ureilite meteorites (NWA 3140 and NWA 4231) plot over a large range of peak centers and FWHMs (1575 to 1595 cm−1 and 35 to 102 cm−1, respectively) reflecting multiple populations of carbon within the samples, including graphite phases (10). Supplementary Text and table S3 provide peak parameters and sample information for points presented in Fig. 5. Different types of carbon measured in reference samples exhibit overlapping band parameters, complicating attribution of a given set of band parameters to any unique carbon source or setting. The peak centers and FWHM from Apollo Temple, Walhalla Glades, and Cheyava Falls G-­bands overlap with at least one example of each organic carbon type, with the exception of graphite. G-­band mineral and textural associations G-­band spatial associations with specific minerals and textural features, together with knowledge of the rock’s deposition and alteration history, can provide contextual information on the nature of the MMC [e.g., (7, 33)]. The rocks of Bright Angel are composed of fine particulate sediment that is hypothesized to have been deposited from suspension (23, 24). The source of the sediments is currently unresolved, but the silicate mineralogy of the primary grains suggests an igneous provenance, with carbonates and sulfates representing a discrete set of minerals that mark the interaction of the primary rock or sediment with surficial or subsurface fluids. Evidence for such aqueous alteration has been previously observed in igneous martian meteorites (8, 15, 41), widely across the surface of Mars (42), and locally in Jezero crater (19, 43). Characterizing the G-­band spatial distribution and mineral and textural associations may help constrain the source and alteration history of organics at Bright Angel. Interpretation of spatially resolved G-­band spectral variability is based on analyses described in Materials and Methods. A subset of points within spectral maps exhibiting G-­bands were identified using two techniques to verify consistency: (i) a spectral feature intensity ranking algorithm and (ii) PCA and k-­means cluster analysis. G-­band peak parameters derived from a subset of points within SHERLOC Bright Angel hyperspectral maps are presented in Fig. 5 (Tables 1 and 2). The most intense G-­band spectra in the Apollo Temple abrasion are associated with a carbonate mineral phase (Fig. 2A), and the mean of these points plots closest to the abiotic carbonate-­associated G-­band in martian meteorite ALH 84001 (Fig. 5) (8, 15). There is also a G-­band association with a sulfate mineral phase (Fig. 2B), but the G-­band is less intense compared to the carbonate association (Fig. 2, A and B). The most intense G-­band spectra in the Cheyava Falls natural surface measurements do not appear to be associated with specific minerals or resolvable textures, but this is likely due to the fine-­grained nature of the rock’s matrix which is at or below the ACI resolution. In addition, observations are further complicated by the higher focus offset (1.7 to 2.2 mm) during data collection compared to other targets, which increases the size of the annular beam at the target and reduces the observed Raman spectral intensity (Table 1). The most intense G-­band spectra in the Walhalla Glades abrasion are associated with the lighter-­toned matrix, and the mean of these points plot closest to the silicified microbialites from (38). This fine-­grained textural association indicates that MMC occurs within the rock’s primary mineral matrix, which PIXL data suggest is a relatively uniform silicate mixed with carbonate and sulfate (24). SHERLOC did not detect a G-­band within the black iron phosphate-­rich grains of Walhalla Glades, and a higher iron concentration in these minerals relative to the surrounding lighter-­toned matrix (24) could attenuate the spectral response through UV absorption of the signal to undetectable levels (44). The association of MMC with both primary and secondary mineral phases suggests possible relationships with depositional and diagenetic processes. Potential MMC relationships to depositional processes include the following: (i) the MMC originated from the igneous protolith sediment, or (ii) during sediment deposition in the lake (25), organic matter in the water column was incorporated between the settling sediments and lithified concurrently with the mudstones. In addition, or alternatively, MMC may have been deposited during one or more diagenetic events involving subsurface fluids. Potential MMC relationships to diagenetic events include the following: (i) early stage diagenetic fluids that facilitated the infiltration

and emplacement of organic matter into the silicate-­dominated matrix, (ii) diagenetic fluids related to the precipitation of carbonate and/or sulfate phases may have mobilized organic matter from an unknown source and simultaneously deposited it with the mineral(s), or (iii) organic matter may have been introduced during late-­stage diagenesis—post carbonate and sulfate precipitation—linking it with both primary and secondary minerals. It remains uncertain how many diagenetic events altered the mudstones of Bright Angel and what order they occurred in, or if the same diagenetic fluids altered the Cheyava Falls and Walhalla Glades rocks. While these scenarios offer insights, none conclusively identify the source of the MMC, and only speculate on the potential timing of its emplacement.

G-­band detections on a dust-­cleared mudstone The detection of G-­bands on the Cheyava Falls rock’s dust-­cleared surface represents the shallowest detection of MMC on Mars. SHERLOC’s penetration depth is dependent on the material analyzed and can be more than 500 μm in martian laboratory analogs (11, 45); however, the majority of Raman scattered photons originate from shallower depths. The surface of Mars experiences factors destructive to organics that include oxidants produced by atmospheric photochemical processes, charged particle radiation, and solar UV ≥190 nm (46, 47). While charged particles can reach depths of several meters (46), UV photons only penetrate the top several millimeters (48), making UV degradation a relevant factor regarding the surface detection on the Cheyava Falls rock. The nature of the organic material as originally formed and deposited may be significantly different from the organics observed at present by SHERLOC, following billions of years of martian geologic history. For example, MMC can form through diagenesis and catagenesis, combined with radiolysis from cosmic rays (49, 50). These processes may have transformed abiotic short-­chain alkanes and alkenes, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, carboxylic acids, amino acids, or other functionalized soluble molecules into the highly aromatized MMC observed on Mars today (51). Protective and stabilizing factors, including dust cover, photoprotective minerals, and the structure of the MMC itself, can prevent or slow UV degradation of organics; these factors are discussed below. The MMC at the Bright Angel outcrop may have been sufficiently shielded by iron-­rich regolith, which reduced exposure to UV radiation (45, 52) and atmospheric oxidation (47), and may only have been relatively recently exposed through aeolian erosion and exhumation. Martian regolith cover, although possibly transient and varying in thickness over geologic time, may need only to be 100 μm thick to offer partial UV radiation shielding (45), and 1 to 2 mm thick for more substantial shielding (53). Regolith shielding may have been thick enough to reduce UV-­oxidation products such as atmospheric H2O2 that reach the surface or near surface (micrometers to millimeters) of the Bright Angel rocks. However, because of limited numerical models, the estimated diffusion depth of atmospheric H2O2 into regolith is poorly constrained and may range from a few centimeters to hundreds of meters [(47) and references therein] and consequently does not constrain the regolith thickness necessary for preservation. In addition, photodegradation may be further inhibited by organic-­mineral interactions, as often observed when organic molecules are adsorbed onto clays—the minerals found in mudstones like Cheyava Falls—which can provide mechanical shielding by enclosing organic molecules inside the mineral’s interlayer spaces [(54) and references therein].

Last, it may be possible that the type of MMC at Bright Angel has a significantly longer lifetime in the Martian ambient environment. For example, the MMC in the SaU 008 meteorite calibration target aboard the Perseverance rover has a G-­band measured by SHERLOC that has persisted over hundreds of sols (55). Laboratory analog studies on UV-­organic interactions are largely focused on labile, soluble compounds mixed with mineral or rock powders [e.g., (45, 52, 54, 56)], which may not represent the expected lifetime of indigenous MMC contained in natural heterogeneous rocks. In addition, the MMC structure itself can impart protection from degradation; in particular, polymerization into macromolecules may increase the resistance of organic matter to radiolysis (50). Notably, the detection of macromolecules on Mars (3) and in surface particles returned from asteroid Ryugu (57) suggests that macromolecules are more recalcitrant and less likely to undergo degradation from both charged particle and short-­wavelength UV irradiation compared to more labile molecules. It is plausible that the Bright Angel outcrop was relatively recently exhumed and that the detected organic matter is recalcitrant, but without knowledge of the outcrop’s age, timing of organic deposition, and thickness of regolith coverage over time, it is not possible to determine radiation exposure times. It is also possible that the organic matter detected on the rock surface is distinct from that detected 7.8 mm below the surface on the abrasion due to differences in organic degradation at different depths. However, the high uncertainty of the Bright Angel G-­band peak parameters, resulting from the noisy nature of the spectra due to operational conditions at the time of data acquisition (see Table 1 and Materials and Methods), precludes this evaluation, and we are therefore unable to characterize organic alteration as a function of depth on the Cheyava Falls rock.

Comparisons to other SHERLOC observations In the subsequent sections, we compare SHERLOC observations at Bright Angel to other mudstone targets and a previous G-­band detection (20) in Jezero crater. Jezero delta fan front Mudstones were previously encountered at the delta fan front within the “Shenandoah” formation (58, 59). Two abraded mudstones were analyzed by SHERLOC: “Berry Hollow” (sol 513) at the “Wildcat Ridge” outcrop and “Uganik Island” (sols 614 to 620) at the “Hidden Harbor” outcrop. Out of 600 spectral points across six maps within the Berry Hollow abrasion, and 800 spectral points across eight maps within the Uganik Island abrasion, no obvious G-­bands were observed in either rock (60). Bright Angel and Shenandoah are both sedimentary mudstones; however, their mineralogy and composition are different. Bright Angel mudstones have a silicate-­dominated matrix composed of fine-­grained aluminosilicate clays and an igneous glass and/or feldspar phase, while Shenandoah mudstones have a sulfate-­rich matrix (24, 61). The Bright Angel mudstone matrices also contain fine-­ grained carbonate and sulfate, and veins of sulfate. The Shenandoah mudstones matrices also contain Fe-­Mg phyllosilicates and sulfate veins (62). While Bright Angel clays are hypothesized products of chemical weathering, it is unclear whether Shenandoah clays are products of alteration, direct precipitates, or detrital in origin (24, 61). Assuming a primary mineral matrix, the difference in matrix and silicate composition suggests different source(s) of sediments between the two formations.

There are also notable differences in the sulfate phases between the two formations. Bright Angel is predominantly composed of Ca-­ sulfate, while Shenandoah sulfates vary in composition (Ca, Fe-­Mg, and ferric) and hydration state (24, 27, 61). At Bright Angel, anhydrous sulfate is detected in the matrix, and hydrated sulfate, consistent with bassanite, was only detected in the Steamboat Mountain abrasion where it occurs as rims around olivine grains (fig. S2). Anhydrite is detected in the matrix at Shenandoah while weakly hydrated sulfate is detected within vein interiors and rims (60). The amount and variety of sulfate phases observed in the Shenandoah formation are interpreted as evidence for sulfate formation from multi­ple fluid and/or evaporation events at the delta fan front (58, 59, 61). In addition, SHERLOC spectra show strong and pervasive sulfate-­ associated fluorescence in the Shenandoah mudstones but not at Bright Angel (60). The sulfate-­associated doublet fluorescence at 305 and 325 nm in the Shenandoah mudstones is likely due to cerium(3+) in the sulfates (21). Notably, the Shenandoah mudstones exhibit variations in doublet fluorescence intensity associated with different sulfate domains (matrix versus vein) (60). The differences observed in textures, minerals, and fluorescence between the mudstones at Neretva Vallis and the delta fan front likely record different depositional and alteration histories. Such differences suggest variation in local alteration settings instead of regional, crater-­wide alteration event(s). Jezero crater floor A G-­band was previously detected in the “Montpezat” abrasion (sol 349) at the crater floor in a single point out of 100 points in a 7 mm– by–7 mm map (20). The rock, from the “Rimplas” outcrop located in the “Máaz” formation, is an aqueously altered igneous rock dominated by pyroxene and plagioclase (1, 19). SHERLOC detected silicate, minor carbonate, and perchlorate or phosphate minerals (29). The mean spectrum of the map exhibits a relatively strong broad band centered at ~1050 cm−1, consistent with igneous glass and/or feldspar (plagioclase) (25, 29). However, the detected G-­band is colocated with a broad peak centered at ~1080 cm−1, which is consistent with carbonate, and the broadness of the feature is consistent with igneous glass and/or plagioclase (20, 25, 29). This possible spectral mix of silicate and carbonate in the rock is comparably similar to that observed in the rocks of Bright Angel, specifically Apollo Temple (Fig. 2). However, the matrix at Bright Angel and groundmass of the Máaz formation likely contain a mixture of silicate phases, making it challenging to pinpoint the specific phase associated with the G-­band. For example, the PIXL XRF maps of Montpezat reveal a mix of alkaline plagioclase feldspar, a fine-­grained KSi-­rich residual melt, and a secondary FeSi-­rich phase from serpentinized Fe-­rich olivine (29, 63). Although the G-­band association with silicate and carbonate in both the Máaz formation and Bright Angel is intriguing, it is difficult to draw conclusions based on this alone, especially considering a G-­band was detected at only a single point in the Máaz formation. In addition, the igneous Máaz formation and sedimentary Bright Angel formation both exhibit a diversity of secondary minerals, indicating that both underwent multiple aqueous alteration events. Specifically, Máaz shows evidence of olivine carbonation-­serpentinization and void-­filling salt (phosphate and perchlorate) precipitation (1, 63). In contrast, Bright Angel shows evidence of extensive vein-­filling salt precipitation (sulfate) from sulfate-­rich fluids. The relative ages of these formations and their sequence of aqueous alteration events are still unconstrained, making it challenging to speculate on organic carbon synthesis, transport, and preservation pathways.

On the basis of differences in texture and mineralogy between the Bright Angel, Shenandoah, and Máaz formations, it is likely that each formation experienced multiple localized aqueous alteration events with varying fluid compositions. However, we note that the comparisons discussed above are limited to SHERLOC observations with scan size areas of 1 mm by 1 mm at minimum. This may include data bias due to the selected mapped areas (e.g., primary matrix versus secondary vein). As such, we use caution when making any conclusive statements on geologic units to avoid overinterpretation from limited spatial coverage.

Astrobiologically compelling sample The Bright Angel rocks within Neretva Vallis contain the most robust and ubiquitous organic detections relative to other targets that have been measured in Jezero crater by SHERLOC. These detections also represent an organic-­bearing mudstone more than 3500 km away from the detections reported from Curiosity rover measurements in Gale crater, which indicates that the habitability of Mars, and the availability of organics, may have been widespread across the planet billions of years ago. Potential organic emplacement (exogenous) and formation processes (endogenous) include the following: carbonaceous interplanetary dust particles and meteoritic infall, in situ synthesized abiotic organic matter, and/or in situ synthesized biological material. On the basis of the variety and occurrences of organic carbon in martian samples (3, 8, 16, 34, 41), there are multiple potential pathways to form abiotic organics on Mars, including condensation from igneous systems and associated volatiles, serpentinization, carbonation, and the electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide in aqueous/ hydrothermal fluids (8, 41). The presence of MMC reported in this work cannot be ascribed at this time to any specific formation mechanism; biological, geological, and meteoritic sources of the organics observed are all possible. Further constraining the origin, distribution, and alteration history of the organic carbon observed at Cheyava Falls requires high-­resolution and high-­sensitivity analyses in terrestrial laboratories, which can be facilitated by the return of this sample to Earth.

MATERIALS AND METHODS SHERLOC The SHERLOC instrument is a DUV Raman spectrometer mounted to the robotic arm of the Perseverance rover, with two context imagers: the ACI—a 10.1-­μm/pixel monochromatic camera—and the WATSON camera (11). SHERLOC Raman and fluorescence hyperspectral map measurements are collected on natural and abraded surfaces. Abraded surfaces are generated with the arm-­mounted drill equipped with the abrasion bit, which exposes a subsurface target 50 mm in diameter and a few millimeters deep for instrument measurements. Both natural and abraded targets are cleared of dust and abrasion tailings by the gas Dust Removal Tool, which puffs compressed gaseous N2 onto the surface in multiple orientations before SHERLOC observations. The SHERLOC DUV NeCu laser irradiates a target with 248.6-­nm photons (as fine as a 110-­μm-­diameter annulus at the surface), generating Raman scattered photons and photons from fluorescence emission of minerals and organic compounds. These photons are collected by the ACI objective lens and injected into the spectrometer optical path and projected onto the 512 pixel–by–2148 pixel

CCD (charge-­coupled device) (11, 64). The first and last 50 columns of pixels are not illuminated. The spectrometer CCD is illuminated in an arc, enabling the CCD columns to be read out in discrete groups of CCD rows (referred to as spectral regions) to allow for variable gain adjustment and limit dark noise (64). Each spectrum region contains 2148 CCD pixels. After a single spectrum is collected, the scanner mirror focuses the laser to a new location on the surface, rastering over a commanded area to build a hyperspectral map.

WATSON WATSON is a copy of the MSL’s Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI) camera (65), capable of acquiring full-­color images focused at infinity to microscopic scales (13 μm/pixel). Bright Angel observations included placing WATSON at working distances (i.e., the distance between the front lens and the image target) of approximately 4 to 40 cm, providing an image resolution from ∼21 to 150 μm/pixel and a field of view that ranges from ~2.5 × 3.3 cm to 18 × 24 cm (11, 66). The rover’s robotic arm can position WATSON to acquire image mosaics, nested image suites of increasing spatial resolution, stereo pair images, and multiposition images for Structure from Motion quantitative surface relief products [(11) and references therein]. WATSON images can be stitched together to create rover self-­portraits and images are also used to colorize grayscale SHERLOC ACI images, yielding a high-­resolution blended composite that captures both texture and color information (67).

Mastcam-­Z Mast Camera Zoom (Mastcam-­Z or ZCAM) is a high-­heritage imaging system based on MSL’s Mastcam, capable of acquiring high-­ resolution panoramic, stereoscopic, and color/multispectral context images of the martian surface (68). Mastcam-­Z consists of a pair of focusable, 4:1 zoomable cameras that provide broadband red/green/ blue and narrowband 400-­ to 1000-­nm color imaging. The cameras can resolve ∼0.7-­mm features at 2 m and ∼3.3-­cm features at 100 m distance, for features ≥5 pixels in size (68). Mastcam-­Z images in Fig. 1 are radiometrically corrected color balanced to show natural color. The Planetary Data System (PDS) file names for images used are provided in table S4.

Spectroscopy data acquisition SHERLOC measurements are collected on natural surface targets and abraded patches after sunset, at favorably cold temperatures to limit the detector’s dark noise. ACI images presented in this manuscript are focus-­stack composite products, which are ground-­generated images incorporating the best-­focus regions within the field of view after aligning the stack of images to correct for lateral offsets. All SHERLOC spectroscopy measurements presented in this manuscript are “detail” scans: 10 × 10 point maps, with 100-­μm spacing between points, and 900 laser pulses at each point. On sol 1024, the SHERLOC ACI focus mechanism experienced a failure that prevented operation of the instrument’s autofocus capability. Anomaly recovery activities resulted in a static fixed-­focus instrument that can be successfully focused using robotic arm positioning. Perseverance’s robotic arm is capable of placing SHERLOC normal to the target with an accuracy of <0.3 mm, depending on the mode of operation used for the target measurement, and retreating from the surface in steps of <0.25 mm. In cases where a ground-­in-­the-­ loop cycle is possible, an ACI imaging z-­stack of a target is performed to determine the best focus placement, with follow-­up spectroscopy
