For Bright Angel targets, the close approach placement to the target surface was 39.6 mm, with the robotic arm moving away from the target in 0.25-­mm steps to a final working distance of 43.35 mm (with a total of 16 steps and 16 images acquired). A systematic offset to SHERLOC focusing from sols 1180 to 1233 resulted in Bright Angel measurements collected, at an average of 1.65 ± 0.4 mm, too close to the target. The SHERLOC spectrometer has a large depth of focus (11) and is relatively insensitive to focus offsets; however, the projected beam diameter overfills the slit when out of focus, resulting in some attenuation of signal. Laboratory and calibration target measurements at various focus positions suggest that a 1.5-­mm focus offset may result in an approximately 35% decrease in signal, where the magnitude of attenuation is dependent on the scattering properties of the sample (Fig. 4 and figs. S6 and S7). Measurements collected out of focus have larger laser beam diameters at the surface, documented in Table 1. In the following sections, we consider SHERLOC optical background signals, focus offsets, detector noise, cosmic rays, and detector hot pixels and discuss how these complicate but do not prevent our mineral assignments.

Focus offset effects on Raman D-­ and G-­bands Focus effects on Raman D-­ and G-­band signals were explored in the laboratory with the SHERLOC Brassboard analog instrument at NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory on several synthetic and natural samples including Murchison meteorite shown in fig. S6B. Further, on sol 1256, SHERLOC analyzed the SaU 008 meteorite calibration target aboard the rover and collected spectra at focus and 1.52 mm out of focus to replicate similar focus offsets during Bright Angel data collection (Fig. 4). Laboratory focus test results showed that when the targets are out of focus by ~1.14 mm, the Raman G-­band intensity decreases by ~50 to 61%, and the G-­band FWHM increases by ~9 to 15 cm−1. The focus offset experiment on Mars resulted in a ~35% decrease in the signal-­to-­noise ratio (SNR) of the SaU 008 pyroxene peak at 1009 cm−1 and showed that out-­of-­focus measurements attenuate the spectral intensity of Raman D-­ and G-­bands by approximately 35%. SHERLOC’s SNR coupled with a decrease in signal intensity make it difficult to determine the presence or absence of a D-­band. Table 1 summarizes the spectroscopy measurements and associated focus plane offsets for each Bright Angel measurements discussed in this work.

Spectroscopy data processing methods SHERLOC data presented in this manuscript are processed with Python scripts using standard Python modules as described below. Spectral data are read from the CCD and binned vertically according to the CCD regions defined (11). Three spectral regions were used for data collected in this manuscript, and all processing below is applied only to “region 1”—the Raman region (800 to 4000 cm−1) of the detector. Spectral “region 2” and “region 3” make up the fluorescence region (~265 to ~355 nm) and are discussed in the “Fluorescence” section of the Supplementary Text. Active (CCD integration with laser firing) and dark (CCD integration with the laser disabled)

spectra are collected in sequence at each spatial point on the surface, and the dark spectrum is used to subtract the spectral background from the active spectrum. Spectra are then filtered to remove data points collected at warm detector temperatures (Table 1), and cosmic rays are removed from spectral maps. Raman peak fitting and peak confidence calculations are performed on spectra following these data processing steps. Laser normalization and background subtraction processing steps each amplify spectral noise and are therefore not applied to most spectral processing in this manuscript, with exceptions described below. The SHERLOC optical background is effectively accounted for by deconvolving the fully constrained Si-­O peak with the ~1600-­cm−1 spectral feature. Below, we provide more detail on each of the steps outlined above. Spectrometer CCD temperature and dark noise The SHERLOC spectrometer CCD is passively cooled and transfers heat to a heatsink phase-­change material containing n-­decane (with a melting point of −30°C) to provide a stable thermal environment for spectroscopy measurements (11). Long measurements and operational restrictions resulted in some datasets collected in nonideal, warmer environments. The spectrometer CCD is nominally read out at −28°C for the entire hyperspectral map acquisition. The contribution of detector dark noise increases with increasing detector temperature and, in some cases, overwhelms the signal. The spectrometer CCD temperature is not reported with every point, but the temperature can be inferred from the median noise in the dark frame. We exclude all spectra collected with a median dark frame value higher than 1730 counts, which approximately corresponds to detector temperatures warmer than −28°C. Table 1 reports the temperature ranges that the CCD experienced during the scan and the number of spectra used in averaging. Laser normalization per map During a SHERLOC spectroscopy measurement, the laser and laser power supply gradually warm, producing fewer 248.6-­nm photons during each pulse. An internal laser photodiode measures the intensity variability of the laser signal for each pulse in a hyperspectral map acquisition, which can enable a spectral correction for relative laser intensity variability within a map, as described in Eq. 1, where Ii is the signal intensity for point i and pi is the photodiode intensity for point i. Corrections for laser intensity between targets is not possible due to site-­dependent factors that can affect the photodiode response, including ambient temperature and surface reflectivity. A laser normalization correction is necessary when comparing the signal intensity of spectra features within a map (as shown in Fig. 2), but for the bulk spectra of each target presented in Fig. 3, laser intensity correction is unnecessary and is therefore not applied. The relative photodiode signal trend for measurements collected under an ideal thermal environment with the same laser pulses per point is similar, and the laser output attenuation is therefore expected to be consistent for mean spectra collected for each target and arm-­stowed optical background measurement presented in this manuscript

Cosmic ray removal The cosmic ray removal technique developed for SHERLOC (69) can be ineffective for datasets collected in environments with a high cosmic ray flux and with long integration times, such as some 900 pulses per point measurements collected at the Bright Angel outcrop.

Identifying and replacing many nearby cosmic rays within a single spectrum can introduce spectral artifacts, complicating the classification of Raman peaks in spectra with many noise spikes. Instead of an identification and replacement cosmic ray removal method, we applied a 5% trimmed mean to each 1 mm–by–1 mm detail map, where the highest and lowest 5% of points are removed before calculating the mean spectrum. A 5% value for the trimmed mean will not remove ubiquitous spectral signals, and empirically, cosmic rays are unlikely to strike the same detector CCD column (within the narrow Raman region of the detector) multiple times during different integrations for a 100-­point map. Hot pixel analysis (described below) and PCA (described in the Supplementary Text) are exceptions to trimmed mean cosmic ray removal processing. Hot pixel analysis characterizes the SD of intensity values on a CCD pixel, and a single cosmic ray noise spike can skew the results. The replaced intensity value is not considered in the hot pixel map analysis. PCA spectral variance is dominated by cosmic rays in uncorrected datasets. Identification of variance within the Raman region to verify the results of the intensity ranking algorithm requires preprocessing to remove cosmic rays. Background subtraction The fused silica window, the front optical element of the SHERLOC spectroscopy and ACI system, generates a persistent optical background signal that contributes to surface measurement spectra (30). The fixed-­focus SHERLOC working distance is closer than the pre-­ sol 1024 measurements, and therefore, the fused silica window is closer to the SHERLOC laser focus point than measurements collected in the previous autofocus operations mode. More Raman scattered photons from the fused silica window therefore reach the detector, contributing to a stronger background signal in spectra collected after the failure of the ACI focus mechanism on sol 1024. A series of new spectral background measurements were collected in the fixed-­focus operations mode using the same Bright Angel laser and spectroscopy configurable parameters to characterize this instrument background signal. The fused silica background contribution is independent of the working distance of the fixed-­focus spectral measurements. As a result of the increased background intensity postanomaly, we observe a weak band at ~1605 cm−1 in the background spectra that was previously not observed. This band is attributed to the overtone of the 800-­cm−1 Si-­O symmetric stretch vibration and coincides with the spectral range of the G-­band feature (70). Arm-­stowed background measurements collected on Mars in a fixed-­focus mode are compared with Corning 7980 fused silica measurements conducted on terrestrial laboratory analog systems, including ACRONM (Analogue Complementary Raman for Operations oN Mars), located at NASA Johnson Space Center, and MORIARTI (Mineralogy and Organics Raman Instrumentation for the Analysis of Terrestrial Illumination), located at the University of Pittsburgh (see fig. S8 and the Supplementary Text for instrument details). Measurements with each system consistently show a 1605/800-­cm−1 overtone/fundamental intensity ratio of 7%. The UV transmission of the SHERLOC fused silica window in the spectral range of the detector is >99.99%; the small contribution of fused silica Raman scattered photons that are reflected from the rock surface back through the instrument is not wavelength dependent, and therefore, rock surface reflectivity does not affect the overtone/fundamental peak ratio. The arm-­stowed optical background measurement is compared with laboratory measurements of Corning 7980 fused silica to validate the calculated peak fit parameters of the ~1605-­cm−1 Si-­O stretching

overtone feature. The laboratory measurements include a contribution from atmospheric O2 at 1555 cm−1, and the Mars arm-­stowed measurements include a contribution from atmospheric CO2 at ~1350 cm−1, which is not present in surface measurements (fig. S8). The optical background peak fit properties (peak location: 1607.54 cm−1; peak FWHM: 125.40 cm−1) are in good agreement with laboratory spectra of the same fused silica used as the front window element on SHERLOC. A fully constrained Gaussian peak representing the ~1605-­cm−1 Si-­O overtone is included as a known contribution to the G-­band peak deconvolution for target spectra. The calculated 1605/800-­cm−1 peak ratio for Bright Angel targets shown in Fig. 3 is significantly higher than 7%, indicating that Raman scattered photons from the surface must contribute to the signal at ~1600 cm−1. The optical background contribution can be corrected by subtracting the mean optical background signal from each spectrum or by modeling the ~1600-­cm−1 signal as the sum of the 1605-­cm−1 SiO overtone and a band from the target. The optical background spectrum has a signal SD of 2.8 counts, which contributes to the target signal when subtracted (30). We therefore deconvolve the ~1600-­cm−1 feature into component peaks to derive G-­band peak parameters to limit the introduction of spectral noise. Peak fitting of Raman bands SHERLOC Raman band parameters presented in this manuscript are calculated from least squares fitting Gaussian functions to the optical background signal and G-­band in the spectral data. Laboratory Raman G-­band results are calculated from least squares fitting Gaussian functions using a single peak (G-­band) or by deconvolving multiple peaks with contributions from a D-­band (2 peaks), a D-­ band and an atmospheric O2 line (3 peaks), or a D-­band, O2 line, and carbonate ν3 peak (4 peaks) using the curve_fit function in the scipy.optimize package. The MMC structure consists of a mixture of sp2 and sp3 hybridized carbons bonded in a variety of organic structures with substituted heteroatoms (17). Because G-­bands derive from an amorphous solid that lacks spatial order and long-­range translational symmetry, the Raman spectrum observed originates from the vibrational density of states of the solid modified by the resonance Raman enhancement of each state (17). Therefore, the classical Gaussian, Lorentzian, and Voigt Raman band fitting functions do not model the physics of the MMC Raman spectrum, and any functional fit to the spectrum is a purely empirical method of quantitatively comparing MMC spectra (17, 71). Simpler fits are preferred, as more variables in the fit increases the number of solutions to the least squares algorithm and increases the uncertainty in the peak fit parameters. The peak fit parameters presented in Fig. 5 are derived from the observed Raman bands (72); currently, Raman bandwidth calibration techniques used to derive the intrinsic Raman band are only developed for homogeneously broadened bands (73), though the instrument slit function may also have an effect on heterogeneously broadening bands like that of the ~1600-­cm−1 feature (72). The terrestrial analog instruments have smaller slit functions than SHERLOC (34.1 cm−1), and therefore, the SHERLOC observed Raman band FWHM is expected to be higher than laboratory instruments, as demonstrated by the peak fit parameters of the HOPG measurements presented in Fig. 5. Spectrometer CCD hot pixel analysis Hot pixels and noise variability on the spectrometer CCD can increase the uncertainty in the assignment of spectral features in some CCD channels. The mean SD of the 25 pixels comprising the ~1600-­ cm−1 feature in the dark frame of the arm-­stowed background measurements is 336 counts. For comparison, the mean SD of dark frame pixels in a 25-­pixel segment of the quiet region of the spectrometer CCD is 370 counts, and is 440 counts in all region 1 pixels. The consistent signal in the dark frame of the 1600-­cm−1 region suggests that hot pixel variance is unlikely to strongly contribute to false-­positive classifications of peaks within this region, which agrees with analysis of anomalous pixel locations reported earlier in the mission (30). Furthermore, spectra presented in this manuscript are means of many points within a map, which decreases potential contributions from individual outliers from anomalous pixels. Mean spectra of a subset of a SHERLOC map may include contributions from hot pixels that persist after applying a trimmed mean to the reduced dataset. Hot pixels vary slowly over the length of the mission (30); during the exploration of Bright Angel, the brightest hot pixels (more than 3 SDs above the mean dark frame variance) within the 900–1900-­cm−1 Raman region at Walhalla Glades were located at 1019 and 1700 cm−1, and those for Apollo Temple were located at 1439, and 970 cm−1, listed in decreasing intensity. Figure S4 shows the SD of the variance of the region 1 dark frame values from all spectra collected at Bright Angel (sols 1180 to 1224). Spectral regions of interest discussed in this manuscript are highlighted in gray; there are two hot CCD pixels (defined as pixels where the variance is more than 2 SDs above the mean dark frame variance) in the phosphate region, decreasing confidence in phosphate peak assignment, but no hot pixels in the sulfate, carbonate, or G-­band spectral regions. We note that phosphate was detected with the PIXL instrument in colocated scans with SHERLOC (25). Intensity filtering algorithm for mineral and organic spatial distribution Figure 2 and figs. S2, S3, and S5 show the mineral and organic spatial associations in Apollo Temple, Cheyava Falls, and Walhalla Glades datasets. Annuli (depicted as hollow circles with varying opacity in the figures) represent the highest 15% of points within a map associated with a Raman feature, sorted by the strength of that feature. Points within a map are ranked by their median baseline-­subtracted intensity within a defined Raman spectrum range, filtering for spectra

that contain cosmic rays and noise spikes within this subset of spectrometer CCD pixels. Annuli opacity is higher for higher ranked points; opaque points represent the strongest signals within the subset of ranked points. Annuli represent the size of the SHERLOC laser spot, with the majority of 248.6-­nm incident laser photons falling within the ~20-­μm annulus width. Figure 2A and fig. S3 show the Apollo Temple G-­band peak intensity distribution, where the selected Raman region is the fitted G-­band peak position and FWHM (1591 and 136 cm−1). Points are not obviously clustered around any resolvable textural features in the colorized ACI image; however, the trimmed mean spectra of the highest 15% of points (42 points for Apollo Temple) show a stronger and broader G-­band signal compared to the mean G-­band for the entire dataset and are associated with a peak present at ~1080 cm−1 attributed to carbonate. Although this peak appears to resemble a hot pixel or cosmic ray, it is more likely associated with the carbonate ν1 vibrational mode. The intensity filtering algorithm for the carbonate-­associated G-­ band spectra is only sensitive to the G-­band spectral region—it is not filtering for high-­intensity carbonate peaks, which could preferentially identify spectra with higher detector noise or cosmic rays. No known detector hot pixels exist on the spectrometer CCD in this region; the expected signal variance inferred from dark spectra noise in this spectral region is lower than the observed peak intensity. As shown in fig. S4, CCD pixel noise variability is independent of proximity to other hot pixels. The ~1080-­cm−1 peak is composed of multiple pixels with relatively high intensity, making it less likely to be associated with a detector hot pixel, which vary independently of each other. The high-­intensity G-­band and ~1080-­cm−1 peak association persists after performing a 45% trimmed mean (removing the highest and lowest 18 spectra), indicating that this feature exists in at least half of spectra containing the highest-­intensity G-­bands and is not a single high-­intensity cosmic ray skewing the mean. A cosmic ray preferentially strikes the same spectrometer detector pixel columns in only the active frame in more than 19 of the 42 spectra, and those 19 spectra coincidentally being associated with the highest-­intensity G-­ band peaks is exceedingly unlikely. Alternative hypotheses for the ~1600-­cm−1 Raman feature detected in rocks at Bright Angel We first considered whether the ~1600-­cm−1 feature could be an instrumental artifact related to the recent change to SHERLOC operations. In addition to the >99% confidence of the ~1600-­cm−1 feature in the trimmed mean Apollo Temple spectrum, the sequence of target analyses further enhances our confidence in the detection of the candidate G-­band indicative of organics. The ~1600-­cm−1 feature

was identified in spectra of rocks within the Bright Angel outcrop, but between the analyses of the Walhalla Glades rock and Cheyava Falls rock, the spectra collected in an abrasion on the Steamboat Mountain rock, which is next to Cheyava Falls (Fig. 1C), show no statistically significant features in the 1600-­cm−1 region, providing a useful negative control for the observations at Apollo Temple and Walhalla Glades. Furthermore, no comparable features are detected in the 1600-­cm−1 region during instrument calibration arm-­stowed scans conducted on sols 1195, 1210, 1222, and 1224, or in the analyses of the SHERLOC calibration targets (SCT) on sol 1211 (SCT Teflon) and sol 1234 (SCT AlGaN). Significantly, the SaU 008 meteorite onboard SHERLOC’s external calibration target serves as an important calibrant for DUV Raman and fluorescence spectra of Mars-­relevant minerals and organics (64, 75). For this study, the G-­band in the SaU 008 target serves as a positive control of a confirmed organic carbon peak. The SaU 008 meteorite showed a G-­band at 1603 cm−1 and an FWHM of 76 cm−1 from sol 935, whereas a measurement taken from a different area of the target on sol 712 showed a G-­band center at 1597 cm−1 and an FWHM of 100 cm−1 (Supplementary Text and Figs. 5 and 6). On sol 1256, measurements of the SCT meteorite do show a well-­characterized G-­band at 1599 cm−1, which is known to be representative of organic carbon in this calibration target, demonstrating a positive control for the ~1600-­cm−1 feature. This combination provides a statistically strong set of spectroscopic observations that is potentially robust to both false-­positive and false-­negative detections of the ~1600 cm−1 band that we attribute to MMC. We considered and ruled out multiple alternatives to the MMC G-­band explanation, as described below.

Fused silica optical background The front optical element of SHERLOC, which is part of the instrument background signal, is a fused silica window that generates a weak band at ~1605 cm−1 attributable to an overtone of the 800-­cm−1 band of silica (70). The intensity ratio of the 1605/800 peaks in the fused silica background is ~0.07, while in the Apollo Temple spectra, this ratio is ~0.52; thus, the fused silica background might contribute to the ~1600-­cm−1 feature, but it is not strong enough to account for the majority of the ~1600-­cm−1 feature. Another phase must be responsible for this feature. Mineral contributions Numerous minerals exhibit minor Raman overtone modes in the 1600-­cm−1 region; however, associated fundamental vibrational modes would be expected to exhibit higher intensity peaks. For example, carbonate minerals have minor Raman modes at ν3 (at ~1443 cm−1) and ν1 + ν4 (~1763 cm−1), which are 9× to 48× less intense than the ν1 mode (~1080 to 1099 cm−1) (25, 76). Previous carbonate detections with SHERLOC on Mars have shown the ν1 mode but not the minor peaks (19, 27, 29); if carbonate were contributing to the ~1600-­cm−1 feature at Apollo Temple, we would expect a stronger corresponding feature for the ν1 mode, which is not observed. Amorphous minerals, such as amorphous carbonates and silicate glasses, have been shown to exhibit broad Raman features compared to crystalline minerals of the same composition (77). The possibility of broad, amorphous carbonate peaks in this region was considered, but visible Raman spectroscopy shows that amorphous carbonate peaks have relatively narrow bandwidths compared to that observed at Bright Angel, and do not exhibit the ν3 and ν1 + ν4 modes (78). The broadness of the ~1600-­cm−1 feature observed in Bright Angel rocks (>100 FWHM) compared to mineral Raman features (<50 FWHM, and based on SHERLOC’s slit width of ~34 cm−1) (64, 72) indicates that the Bright Angel ~1600-­cm−1 feature is not likely a mineral, or a combination of mineral modes. Hydrated minerals and hydroxyl group compounds can give rise to Raman bands in the 1600-­ to 1650-­cm−1 and 3200-­ to 3550-­cm−1 regions, due to H-­O-­H bending and O-­H stretching vibrations, respectively (79). Mineral hydration is characterized by a hydrogen stretching mode in the ~3000 to 3800 cm−1 spectral range, and H-­O-­H bending modes are very weak compared to the strong stretching mode vibrations (25). The Steamboat Mountain target exhibits a hydrated sulfate Raman signal, including a broad hydration stretching mode at ~3600 cm−1 and a bending mode at ~1646 (±10.1) cm−1 (fig. S2). Notably, there are no observed hydration stretching modes in the 3200-­ to 3550-­cm−1 region in any of the other targets at Bright Angel; thus, any contribution from bending modes in the 1600-­cm−1 region that could complicate the G-­band assignment are, in the upper limit, at the level of the noise in our measurements. Contamination Last, we note that terrestrial organic contamination is unlikely and does not adequately explain the observed diversity in G-­band signals across Apollo Temple, Cheyava Falls, and Walhalla Glades, or the absence of such signals in other martian rocks and SHERLOC calibration targets. The SHERLOC instrument never makes contact with the surface of a rock, and the abrasion bit used for Apollo Temple was cleaned and sterilized before launch (80) and is the same bit used on other abrasions in Jezero Crater, none of which exhibit the same band strength as that observed in Apollo Temple.

Image processing methods See tables S1 and S2 for a list of WATSON and ACI imaging observations at the Bright Angel outcrop. Target topography via ACI focus merge products In some cases, intensity variability could be attributed to rough sample surfaces, where points at better focus produce higher spectral signal than points collected out of focus (Fig. 4 and figs. S6 and S7). For Apollo Temple and Walhalla Glades measurements, ACI z-­stack images may be used to build a topographic map of the interrogated area of an image to evaluate the contribution that focus changes have on spectra within a map. The same focus merge program used onboard Perseverance and Curiosity to merge WATSON and MAHLI images (65) is used to create best-­focus ACI image products along with topographic map products generated on Earth from the ACI z-­stacks. The topographic variability within detail maps in the Apollo Temple abrasion patch is <0.37 and <0.035 mm in the Walhalla Glades abrasion patch detail map, determined from ACI range map products (65). The ACI’s horizontal resolution (10.1 μm/pixel) and overlapping focus intervals (depth of field = ±0.25 mm) and arm motion steps (0.25 mm) enable interpolation of per-­pixel focus position with sub–0.25-­mm precision. Considering the magnitude of this relatively small relief and the expected intensity attenuation at this scale (<10%), the observed spectral intensity variability for these targets cannot be due to minor changes to instrument focus caused by sample topography. Furthermore, the low background fluorescence points in Apollo Temple (fig. S9) are better focused than the average point within the detail maps, providing further confidence that the signal variability is attributed to the intrinsic properties within the sample, and not focusing effects. Colorized ACIs Colorized ACIs are produced by first aligning a WATSON image to an ACI image and then applying a color conversion using the hue and saturation values from the WATSON image and intensity values from the grayscale ACI image. Colorized ACIs yield a high-­resolution blended composite that captures both texture and color information. Colorized ACI methodology is fully described in Sharma et al. (67). WATSON self-­portrait Perseverance’s self-­portrait of the Beaver Falls workspace (Fig. 1C) was taken on sol 1218 and is made up of 62 individual WATSON images stitched together using the same method used by the MSL MAHLI camera (65).
